100% complete update:

I enjoyed this game when it was in EA, but I really fell in love with it when I came back to play the release version. The core mechanics are basically the same, but the details were greatly improved. Each map is unique and interesting and it can be approached as a bunch of individual missions or as part of a larger narrative thread. I really can't recommend this game enough if you are looking for a chill out game or if you are very meticulous. It's not a game for everyone because there isn't any action or enemies, but it's a delightfully unique puzzle-esque game.

This is one of the few games that I wasn't ready to shelve once I 100%'d the achievements and am keeping it installed to hop in occasionally.

I'll admit, I bought this game ironicly.  100+ hours later and I'm considering getting a part time job as a janitor IRL.  There's something seriously zen about mopping up the aftermath of all these 'incidents' and not having to worry about trying to stop them for once!  As a bonus, the devs have a great sense of humor which is sprinkled throughout the various notes and incident reports in each level.

If you're not into the whole zen thing, there's also a p sweet speedrun mode.  There's even character progression of sorts, in that your office is persistant and has its own secrets.

My only complaint is sometimes it's not obvious when my mop is saturated with gore due to colored lighting, but I could probably just pay more attention.

It may not have been the developer's intention, but this game has gone a ways toward keeping me alive.  Dramatic statement, I know, but bear with me.

   I've spent a good chunk of my life grappling with depression.   During a particularly low point, I started trying to go through my Steam Library and get some time in on a bunch of games purchased but unplayed, as one does. I settled on this one after a couple that either frustrated me or failed to keep my attention for long.

   Playing this, especially without giving yourself a time limit, is incredibly relaxing and fulfilling.  I don't even like cleaning in real life, but I can spend hours on this- when I'm not feeling the executive function, this game can allow me to circumvent that.  The messes are lovingly constructed, with meticulous attention to detail, and the solution to any problem is easy to quantify and formulaic, which is exactly what my brain needs when I'm struggling with real life and need a break.  The dystopia that this game inhabits is contextually removed from the horrors that happened just beforehand (though I'll admit, I felt for the union in the Uprinsing level), so every map is like a gory, sloppy, garbage-strewn Easter egg hunt with the freedom to approach it however you want (and the Easter eggs are abundant, whether they be curious items to find in a level, or the stories you can piece together from the scenes you discover and the notes left behind). 

   I've introduced another friend who's in the same psychological boat as me.   If we're both in a low place, this game lets us hang out together despite being on opposite sides of the country, spend a few hours chatting while keeping busy, and leaving feeling like we've accomplished something.

 So, in summary, bulleted list of things I appreciate about this game:
    
  * You set the level of pressure, including 'none'.
  * All problems are surmountable with patience and attentiveness.
  * It's multiplayer, but just as good as a solo experience.
  * Completing tasks gives a sense of accomplishment without stress, and there are practically unlimited ways to get from start to finish.
  * While your toolkit is fairly consistent, the variety of levels (especially with workshop content) keeps things varied.
  * The level design adds engaging narrative and rewards investigation.
 * The achievements encourage nonlinear thinking and and experimentation.
  * The soundtrack is good, and if you don't like it, you can always throw the boombox into the incinerator.

Did you play DOOM when it was released in the 90s?  What about the original Half-Life or Unreal?  Did you ever wonder who the heck's gonna clean up after these heroes?

The answer has finally been provided by the developers of VCD, and the answer --- is you.

There is no story.  There is you.  There is a mop.  There is a bucket of water.  You have no idea who is responsible for the carnage; you only know it's your task to clean up after it.

For such a strange idea for a game, the developers have really outdone themselves in my opinion.  They have taken an idea that likely only tugs at the corner of the minds of .01% of the total FPS-gaming population and made a game out of it.  They've made a game that seems incredibly boring actually fun.

As a Janitor for the Viscera Cleanup Detail company, each facility you visit must be painstakingly mopped; all the trash must be picked up; and all the body parts must be incinerated.  How you complete this task is up to you, but that facility had better be spotless when your supervisors arrive, or you risk losing your job (and that's actually an Achievement).

After completing a facility, you return to your "office," and can read reports on your progress.  These reports vary from employee commendations to tongue-in-cheek company newsletters, and really add to the experience.  You are also able to take "trophies" with you should you so choose by placing them in the blue trunk that you take with you to each job.

People who don't enjoy ironic humor, or never played an FPS, should stay well away.  But if you love watching the gibs fly on any contemporary FPS game; or even enjoyed the pixelated trips down Memory Lane of DOOM or Duke Nukem 3D;  or even the bump-mapped polygons of Unreal and Half-Life, this is a must-have in your collection.  You already blew the place to smithereens; didn't you mom teach you pick up after yourself?

BUY THIS GAME. I had had it on my wishlist for a couple years but never put the money down because it seemed like a $2.00 gag game but cost over $10. I liked the concept, but surely the gimmick of cleaning up after the big sci-fi battles would wear off after an hour or two, right? WRONG. This game is everything you didn't know you wanted.

I spent most of my dozens of hours in Skyrim and Fallout collecting and hording cool things, then find places to store them around my house/lair, but I always felt bad at the end because those are supposed to be role-playing games where you save the world and fight bad guys and whatnot, yet here I am organizing closets while dragons wreak havoc on a world already at war. I feel guilty for neglecting my duties, but this is a major plothole in those games because, no matter how many hours I screw off and ignore my responsibilities to save the world, it's always waiting for me, and I can go back to fighting and win the game.

Not in Viscera Cleanup Detail. If you fail to do your job, you are fired. When you're fired, you lose all the customization you've done to your "home" (office). I've never seen such an immersive roleplaying mechanic. There's no "quicksave, destroy everything, laugh at the results, and then go back to normal". The first time I went to my office after the first mission, I incinerated everything in it with a flamethrower, not realizing it was a persistent saved state. Now, ten hours later, I have three Employee of the Month plaques on my wall...and a once-molten pile of metal and circuitry where my computer once was. This teaches a very valuable lesson: in real life, there is no quicksave. You are responsible for your actions and cannot run from the consequences of your psychotic breaks.

Speaking of psychotic breaks, they even simulate the madness you can experience when viewing these horrific scenes in isolation. I hosted an open multiplayer game hoping someone would join, and eventually I started hearing noises, but I couldn't find the other player. I got scared and rushed toward the flamethrower, hoping I would find it before my partner. I would never hurt him with it...I just want to make sure he is as honest as I am. After wandering around scared for 20 minutes, I realized there was nobody there.

I love the realism in this game. Each map has a "Janitor's Trunk" where you can store things you want to take back to your office from the map, but you lose points if you steal company property. I'm hoping to steal a new computer soon (remember that I melted my last one). Actually, "steal" isn't the right word; I deserve to take a bonus after all my hard work. And anyway, the Company usually agrees with me, since they still give me excellent evaluations no matter what. They might fire me if they knew I was stuffing corpses into my Trunk and had an entire storeroom full of human heads propped up on top of their severed feet, but so far I haven't been caught. If you want to do this too, I recommend being careful about it. The Company always lets me get away with a few things because I am so diligent in filling out my incident reports and tidying up the scene.

Part of the appeal of this game may come from the fact that I used to be a medical laboratory janitor myself. While you would think that you're being respectful to the janitor by cleaning up after yourself and always leaving little mess, I actually much preferred it when the scientists left the lab in disarray because it was more exciting. I was always upset when they were tidy because it meant I had nothing to do. Cleaning up chemical spills was always fun. I used to have to imagine what it would be like to clean up the scene of a mutant/alien attack, but now I can visualize it very well and, in fact, act it out in Viscera Cleanup Detail. I'm only 11 hours in, but I am already convinced that VCD should be on the list of top RPGs of all time.

I should list the negatives though:

No option to wash your hands (you will see how this leads to embarassment someday)

Sometimes there will be a scorch mark hidden behind a pipe or foliage that is inaccessible with the tools we have, yet the game still holds me accountable. Just a small minor point off, but the in-game consequences post-level are sometimes dire

I have never seen any public multiplayer games being hosted. I wish more people would play. Feel free to add me and we can clean together!

I would like to see more roleplaying elements. Perhaps contract options - hourly pay for starters, salary for veterans, etc. Use that money to buy bigger buckets, larger office, and the like. Also, what happens after work? Would love to see some play with the balance between working too hard and not spending enough time with your family, and not working hard enough and therefore not being able to support your family properly.

The broom isn't as useful as it should be. It's good for gathering things into one place, but I still have to pick up ammo casings one at a time with my hands because the broom does not push things into boxes very well.

I've only done two levels so far that have aliens, but they both used the same alien model, just with different colorizations. I'd like to see more variety in the aliens. Hopefully I find more later on in the game.

So, if you're the type of person who looks at the reviews first, you might be wondering: What is Viscera Clean-Up detail? To quickly summarize, it's basically a game where you clean up the aftermath of your average old-school FPS level/sci-fi movie mishap. Mopping up blood, burning the remains of gored aliens etc. It's a game almost certainly born from a joke, but it's execution certainly isn't one. You're given a variety of cleaning implements to perform your job, from things as low-tech as a simple, if slightly stylized mop to as futuristic as a laser gun that can mend bullet holes, and actually doing a thorough job takes an understanding of all the gadgets on your toolbelt. 

It's bizarrely relaxing, and perfect for doing things like listening to podcasts or audiobooks over. Much like the games it lampoons there's also plenty of fun secrets to find, including a bunch of momentos you can take back to your office at Aerospace Sanitation and put on display. Speaking of your office, even it has secrets to discover! There's even a sort of larger narrative one can slowly piece together across the game's many levels if they take the time to really search every nook and cranny. It's a lot of fun. This all comes from someone who played the game entirely single player, so I can't speak to the funcitionality or fun factor of the multiplayer personally, but having seen the YouTuber Criken's video on it, I get the impression it's a blast, whether your friends are actually interested in cleaning or not. 

Overall, I'd very much recommend Viscera Clean-Up detail.

I have never hated saviors of mankind as much as I have while picking up their discarded ammo casings and fixing bullet holes in the walls.

Reasons why it's great for co-op:

1.  The satisfaction you and your friends get when seeing actual progress in transforming the unique environment of the game you're playing.  Seriously, this sounds weird, but we feel great seeing what we had to work with and what we made it into.  I never expected to enjoy playing the game as much as I did and I was shocked at how much fun the friends I gave my four pack to liked it.

2.  Hearing them argue about the best methods to dispose of a body (record for blackmail later!).

3.  Seeing them walk into a room, look up, and exclaim, "Oh god...HOW IS THAT EVEN POSSIBLE?!"


Early Access Tips:

Remember, if you play the game now, it's not going to be at its best.  Early access means it's rough and there's definitely some code optimization and collision detection going on that can be frustrating (and sometimes funny as hell) to work with.

When hosting a game, it's a direct connect type.  So make sure the person hosting has a pretty decent computer and a solid internet connection.  If you can't connect to their sever, they may need to setup port forwarding.  The ports used by this game are 7777 and 27015

If you get a "too many actors" error message on your server, it means there's too many unique items.  This can happen from tracking too many player bloody footprints around.  Happened a lot when we were doing a 4-man cleanup team.  To solve this, have someone get rid of all the ammo casings on the ground (pick up and drop in the incinerator) and the rest of the group should focus on getting a specific area of floor clean.  Of all blood and gore.   To prevent this from happening (until it gets fixed) try making little clear footpaths to all the necessary machines (incinerator & bucket maker).

Viscera Cleanup Detail is a fun game to play with friends or listen to something in the background if going solo. For a decade old game, it holds up on the fun factor and looks decent (recommend it on sale). 

That being said it's a shame the game runs poorly by default. To get the most out of the game (and its expansions) you'll need to manually adjust the fps. Go to steam\steamapps\common\viscera\engine\config\BaseEngine.INI (or from your library-properties-installed files-browse). Open this file with Word or Notepad and search for the following: 

bSmoothFrameRate=TRUE
MinSmoothedFrameRate=166 (game will bug if this goes beyond 166- adjust to your liking)
MaxSmoothedFrameRate=166 (game will bug if this goes beyond 166- adjust to your liking)

Now save the file and upon reopening the game you'll have better fps. Many thanks to Churo Zan for posting this in a Steam forum.

Viscera Cleanup Detail is easily one of my most favorite titles of 2014.  From a premise so insanely simple comes one of the most interesting, gloriously monotonous games I have ever had the fortune to play.

As a space-station janitor, your life is a thankless one. Wake up, go to work, come back, get shouted at by manager and go to sleep knowing that the day after will no doubt be exactly the same. So what makes this game so awesome to play? 

This is a game for the people who want something to play, but don't want to work their mind too much... This is a game in which you can watch a TV show, listen to a podcast or some excellent music whilst you play. Many hours have been spent catching up on podcasts and cleaning away to my hearts content.

While it is indeed early access, that should by no means put any potential buyers off, as it is frequently updated with new maps, janitorial tools and in the near future, workshop support, meaning that a multitude of mods will no doubt arrive to spice up the game even further!

In summation, this is an early access game that does it right, in a sea of so many underwhelming titles. I would DEFINITELY recommend it.

First of all, understand what Viscera Cleanup Detail is about: 
You're a space janitor; You have a mess; You must clean the mess- or you'll be fired.

Seems simple enough, but the devil is in the details- and single detail is this: This game is hard. Based solely on the fact that you cannot meander about doing a bit of one thing, and a bit of another; You have to have a strategy on the order in which you do things. You can, and will spend an hour or two on one level- if you let yourself go that far.

"This sounds like a commitment." I hear you say, and yes! It is- and it has to be one that you find enjoyable in order to truly appreciate the subtle fun that this game has to offer.

*This game is fun, because it offers a challenge that current games lack: Self management, and to an extent- self control. 

You will not have some computerized message on-screen to tell you: "Pick up the body parts first" or "Mop a path to the incinerator and bucket dispenser in order to minimize bloody footprints" you learn these things as you go, and you have to be willing to experiment, and keep an open mind in order to succeed.

So, on a closing note- if you like experimenting with processes, as well as organizing yourself in a productive manner- then congratulations! You'll likely enjoy this game a lot!

If you're more the sort who likes to make a mess of things, and loves playing with body parts, and spilling buckets of blood everywhere, then you'll still like the game, but you'll likely get bored of it quicker, and lose friends over playing hockey with an intestine.

Viscera Cleanup Detail is a unique thing. Those of you who've played the gory games like Dead Space, Resident Evil, Silent Hill, will maybe have once joked that you don't envy whoever has to clean the mess up that you, in those games, makes.

Turns out that is EXACTLY the case in VCD. YOU are the shmuck who got sent to the blood-drenched space station AFTER the Bald McAngry Spacemarine protagonist of another adventure had passed through. YOU are the poor sod who has to pick up all the limbs, the guts, the organs, all of it. YOU are the janitorial staff hired to clean up after the incidents.

That is what makes it so oddly satisfying and brilliant all at once. There is no big bad enemy bosses, there is no universe to save, there is no multi-level demon destroying slaughter. There is only you, and the aftermath of the previous examples. Something had happened here, judging by the abundance of guts and trash and casings...but that isn't what you're paid to think about, really. You're cleaning up after the story has happened.

The levels are quite diverse, ranging from a trashy, smelly waste disposal area to an entire digsite or even a zero gravity chamber, all of them filled to the brim with things that need mopped up or incinerated or both. Some even have their own unique gimmick, such as the Sandtraps of Unearthly Excavation that can be fed items, though it may just regurgitate other items and cause further mess.

The game is somewhat passive aggressive in it's design. Your automated waterbucket dispenser can jam and sometimes spew out bodyparts, which can make a mess. Or your Biohazard Bin dispenser can spew out some gibs...which needs cleaned up as well. The game does it's best to let you know that your job is grisly. You will need to take bloody buckets to be incinerated, you will need more buckets to mop up a spilled bucket. You'll need bins to carry all that viscera to the incinerators too...but that might just make more mess if you spill any.

It becomes oddly satisfying to turn a gory scene entirely on it's head. Make everything nice again, put it together, organize boxes. Do well enough and you'll be promoted. Do even better and you'll get an Employee of the Month award! The 'feedback' given to you outside of Speedrun mode gives the game little snippets of flavor. If you do well, you'll receive a meaningless promotion with very minute and insignificant changes to your lifestyle, such as a 5% salary increase, or a slightly bigger locker. Of course, your colleagues begin to hate you for this, because then the company expects higher performance from them too. This has no real changes evident in gameplay, but you CAN collect multiple Employee of the Month awards to decorate your office with...

All in all, VCD is still Early Access but hell, if it can make a strangely tedious job like janitorial work satisfying in a weird way, money well spent.

Also if you see Bob, notify security immediately.

The graphics are surprisingly great, and there's more to it than just mopping up messes and carting out bodies. You get bonuses for repairing level specific objects and stacking things in the right loading areas, or by using a welding gun to melt an eldritch tentacle into a single cauterized blob for easy transport. You can really be very tactical/logical about the whole thing, and for some people - myself included - many hours of slow methodical not-quite-work is a wonderful way of spending the time.

The levels are all interesting and distinct; from the enemies to the colours used in the lighting. There's a bunch of references and homages to horror and scifi throughout the game, and plenty of easter eggs, some you can even take with you to your office to start a trophy room. You're absolutely as much a traveller as a Janitor, it pays to be observant!

Workshop support is icing on the corpse. They even give you a copy of UDK to do your own things, no messing around with loading packages, it all works right from the menu.

Only problem I can see with it is multiplayer isn't especially user-friendly - I've never been on a multiplayer server since the browser doesn't work too good. That or there are no internet servers. LAN probably works fine though!

Viscera Cleanup Detail is a very meditative game in an odd way. It is remarkably stress releiving to systematically mop up all the gore and nasty bits left by our unseen hero's efforts. Highly recommended, both as a fun game and as tool to achieve total mindfullness!

[h1]"This place is a mess" you mutter to yourself, as you sigh and grab your mop.[/h1]

Viscera Cleanup Detail does what it says on the box: you clean up viscera. You travel to a wide variety of locales (this is also true of the DLC, which are thematically brilliant), always with the same mission: restore said location/facility to pristine condition after whatever disaster has taken place. Armed with your trusty mop, and with the help of the bin and bucket dispensers, you set to work, cleaning the entrails, blood, various chunks of body and whatever else might be considered unseemly.

Attention to detail is required to do well in this game, armed with your trusty sniffer to guide you. Often, you will find entrails or blood in the last place you will think to look (granted, this matters most if you are trying to get Employee of the Month on the map in question). Well optimised for the most part, if you look closely enough in the maps you will find tributes to other series (e.g. Half Life, DOOM) scattered around as the game pays homage to iconic items. There is even a speedrunning (speedcleaning?) mode included if you want to test yourself in that department, although I found it to be the opposite of relaxing.

Criticisms? Some. Multiplayer can be hit and miss (might be latency dependent but I had issues connecting to others when I tried, there is a workaround at http://www.runestorm.com/forums/viewtopic.php?t=78301 to force the game to use the native TCP stack rather than Steamworks), the HARM is annoying most of the time as it often gets stuck on nothing and then catapults you and your bins, and the physics engine can be frustrating. Its most noticeable when trying to stack barrels/crates, but you will encounter it frequently when carrying things, trying to fill bins, moving around etc. - it is rage inducing to see a full bin or dirty bucket spill its contents because you "tripped" on a flat surface or because a can is shifting things around inside the bin.

It looks weird, it seems weird, it is a bit weird - but it can be enjoyable, almost therapeutic, to lose yourself for a few hours and take some pride in a job well done. This is a very unique game indeed and is good for some laughs and general chaos. The included Steam Workshop support is the icing on the cake and likely to keep you entertained long after the official maps are done.

So chances are you are looking at this game and thinking "what's the deal with this? Why would I want to be a space janitor?" And first of all, that's Space Sanitation Professional to you. Second, this game is a ton of fun. More fun than it has any right to be. Especially if you play with friends.

In this Space Custodian simulator you play as part of the lowly sanitation crew for an evil corporation in the far future, and you're tasked with cleaning up the messes left behind by horrible plant experiments, alien attacks, mutations gone wrong, etc. You know, normal custodial things. You are the guy who cleans up the mess after the hero of a sci-fi FPS has killed all the bad guys and left. Many of the levels are homages to sci-fi movies (like The Thing or Event Horizon), books (like 20,000 Leagues Under The Sea), and games (like Half-Life). The game is very tongue and cheek, and that's not just because body parts keep coming out of the bucket dispenser. Easter eggs (some literal) and macabre humor abound.

How does the gameplay work? You are tasked with paying proper respect to the deceased (throwing their bodies in the incinerator), picking up garbage, bullet shells, organs, etc, mopping up blood, getting rid of bullet holes, and more. You have several machines that dispense tools, like water buckets and boxes for trash, all of which eventually end up in the incinterator, and a laser gun for getting rid of bullet holes and burning up uncooperative flora and fauna. There are no enemies in the game, but that doesn't mean your teamates won't find ways to get you killed. Everything from explosives to pushing your teammates into environmental traps, to setting up the turret that doesn't like people when no one was looking... Even walking into someone with too much garbage in your crate can get someone killed - the physics engine, like in most simulator games, is pretty wonky, but it isn't a bug, it's definitely a feature.

This game is a ton of fun to play with friends, and it is both simple enough to pick up quickly, and involved enough to keep you coming back. I find that game both relaxing to play when you get into a cleaning groove, and hilarious when you and your friends are finding new ways to sabatoge each others efforts. Even in the best of situations you end up creating an even bigger mess than when you started, but it is very satisfying to gradually whittle away at it until you are finished. There is also a ton of content. I'm twenty hours in, and even though I've replayed a few levels I'm still not all the way through the main game, and there seems to be a ton of fan created content. A great co-op game, I would totally clean up the horrible experiment gone wrong and hide all the evidence before the space police arrive for my evil corporate overlords again.

You play a janitor tasked with cleaning up after the sort of violent incidents we've all come to expect of video games and movies. Scrubbing guts off the walls, floor, and ceiling may seem a straightforward objective, but you'll struggle with zero gravity, belching aliens, still-active defense systems, and, of course, faulty equipment.

The levels, nearly all unique and memorable, are meant to stand alone. You'll find no tedious tutorial, and the muted, epistolary nature of the stories means you or your friends can drop in and out of any map without a care. 

With your trusty janitor's trunk, you can transfer items to and from your own peristent office - a scummy sort of trophy room you might be inclined to decorate and show off. There's also a speedrun mode and a level editor, so the goal is essentially what you make it. Whether you like setting records or slapping your friends with a soiled space mop, there's something here for you.

Played straight, the game might occasionally challenge you, but it's overall just funny, therapeutic, and intensely gratifying to the fastidious completionist. Even after hours of real-life sanitation work, Viscera Cleanup Detail is a joy to come home to. Obviously, it's not for everyone, but I absolutely recommend it to anyone who appreciates a job well done.

A common misconception about the game, partly due to the store page, is that this is a game that is solely about tedious cleanup work. The cleaning aspect of this game is a huge part of the experience. However, as you play, it starts to become a bit more of a puzzle game. Work smarter, not harder. Examine the mess before you and try to come up with more creative or efficient way to tackle the problem. Some levels require breaking tasks down into sections. Other levels require tackling one type of mess at a time. It's a very relaxed experience, but there is a small amount of brainwork.

The hardest part about the game is getting friends to play it with you. They either don't want to buy it, or don't want to play it. I had only a handful of coop sessions, and they were very chill hangouts with me and my coop partners dividing up tasks and supporting each other. Maybe this time I'd ferry supplies to the worksite while another did the cleanup. Maybe one would only handle mopping, and the other only handle trash detail. This was very rewarding and generally entertaining. 


Yet, I still spent most of my time alone. As I played alone, I began to have sobering realizations about the game and its flaws. I played through every level, did every achievement, and completed every challenge available. The experience was a long, often grueling trip, filled with many lows, but almost no highs. I realized, in retrospect, that I was GLAD that I hadn't subjected my friends to each and every level in the game, and I was grateful that the levels we had played together were some of the few decent ones. It was at at that moment I realized I couldn't give this a recommendation.


The gameplay itself is fairly straightforward, and for the most part easy to pick up and play. However, The game actively sabotages itself(or rather, you) in so many ways, and it is does so both intentionally and unintentionally. It's mechanics are so simple, and yet the are so volatile that they feel unfair for no apparent reason.

The majority of your equipment can fail for no reason other than randomness. There are machines that you use to call in new buckets and bins, to help you clean the area. They will occasionally dispense guts and blood instead, only adding to your mess. This might be "cute" or "funny" the first time, but after the 50th, it's pretty much insulting. There is no reason for this mechanic, and there is no "skill" to it either. You will eventually have a malfunction, and no amount of player skill or foresight can avoid it. 

It seems like I'm picking on this one mechanic, but there are several of these kinds of mechanics littered throughout the game. Your tools are constantly working against you for no reason. The fact that their are achievements that highlight these mechanics only furthers how confusingly counter-intuitive it all is.

Imagine playing a modern FPS, and your guns just jammed at random, and you had to spend 15 seconds unjamming them. Imagine playing an RTS, and your soldiers just randomly lost health because they had a predisposed condition for some random disease. Imagine playing an RPG, and your party members just randomly  lost experience points because, "Everyone forgets things from time to time".


Furthering this, many of the maps are designed in such a way that they work against you. Many of the levels are very dark, yet you lack any reliable way to illuminate the area(beyond a finicky neon floor lamp that can break and explode). Some of the levels are entirely made of rusty complicated metal textures. Good luck seeing bullet holes and blood in a mostly dark room that's entirely rust colored and metal plated. Some levels are entirely blue, and all the alien blood is also blue. Some levels are entirely green with tons of plant life(some count as trash, some don't), and all the aliens on those levels have green blood. Some levels have tons of small cracks, and plenty of tiny bullet casings that get lost between them.

Your only method of tracking down all these messes is a tool called the "Sniffer". An obtuse "hot and cold" mechanic, where the closer you are to the mess, the more noise and flashing it makes. In a building with multiple floors and rooms, finding that missing mess could mean you retracking the level multiple times watching the Sniffer like a hawk. Spoilers, it's hiding behind a bunch of vines on a ceiling. Why in God's name we can't have a flashlight, a mess radar, and a blacklight is anyone's guess.


What would the developer response to all of these mechanics be? 

"Cleaning is not easy in real life, nor should it be in a game."
"Being a janitor is tough."
"Your cleaning must be a grueling and unrewarding task."

Summarized directly from their FAQ. Imagine if those were the first few lines on the store page.


Ultimately, I came to the conclusion that the developer doesn't understand the appeal of their game. They have little respect for their concept, and maybe little respect for their player as well. There is a metric ton of potential for a very cool puzzle game here, but it's squandered by poor execution. I wish I could chalk it up to developer inexperience, or merely honest mistakes. No, it's partly deliberate. It is their failure to understand the strengths of their game, and them actively building mechanics and levels that work against those strengths. The Halloween map alone speaks volumes, as it's possibly the magnum opus of everything that is flawed about VCD in one level.

Finally, don't drag your friends into it.

Have you ever needed to occupy yourself with something that could help you wind down and relax? This game is perfect for just that, even when you end up spilling blood and guts all over the cargo bay. There's a certain charm in putting in the time to accomplish such menial tasks while also feeling like you're working toward something - nothing compares to the feeling when you look back on a corridor and it's sparkling clean when an hour ago it was covered in blood.

I normally don't find the idea of cleaning entertaining, but I do find it relaxing, and Viscera Cleanup Detail manages to bring both entertainment and relaxation together in a way that really helps me forget about things for a while.
